title: Coaching Case Studies #4
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the fourth instalment of his coaching series, Barton draws two teaching lessons from lessons he observed. The first and longer case follows a teacher who has made mini-whiteboard mass participation habitual and who asked students for a non-example of a factor of 21; Barton praises the move but notes the non-examples offered were obvious. He suggests sharpening the prompt to 'a non-factor someone might think is a factor' to surface misconceptions, and recommends his 'Give an example of…' framework, whose sequence of simple, harder, interesting and tempting non-examples pushes students toward the boundary of a concept. The second case uses heat maps of teachers' circulation time to show that room layout and habit left some students' work barely seen or not seen at all. His remedies are to remove layout black spots and to plan and rehearse a circulation route that covers every desk. The unifying argument is that checking understanding depends on deliberate design, both of the questions asked and of where the teacher goes.
points: Barton's principle that understanding requires knowing both what a concept is and what it is not underpins his push for well-chosen non-examples.
Asking for a non-example 'someone might think is an example' raises the demand and is designed to expose misconceptions such as multiples, decimals or negative numbers passing as factors.
The 'Give an example of…' grid moves from safe examples to 'interesting' boundary cases and tempting non-examples, with peer marking used to surface disputed answers for discussion.
Heat maps of circulation revealed desks the teachers never reached, so Barton recommends rearranging layout to remove black spots and rehearsing a planned route around the room.
quotes: Previously, he would have asked for volunteers or Cold Called individual students. But he now habitually uses tools of mass participation in order to check both the effort and understanding of all students, instead of hearing from just one or two.
This was fantastic. I am a huge believer that in order to really understand something we must know both what it is and what it is not, hence I love a non-example.

This may also have revealed some misconceptions. If the teacher showcased some of these answers as he did with 24, there may well have been students who disagreed and thought they were factors, and this could have been addressed.

But the third example - an “interesting” example - is where it really kicks off. This is an attempt to elicit a boundary example from students - in other words, how close can they get to the edge of this concept without tipping over into non-examples?

This is clearly an issue because circulation has several benefits. It allows us to check students’ effort, pick up on any misunderstandings, offer words of praise and encouragement, and reduces the chance of poor behaviour.
This is not an argument for groups, by the way. I am a big fan of desks all facing the front, but considering altering the layout to eliminate black spots is key.
